title: 121 sums suffice to find the most common sum for a word and remainder
impact: For a 2,048-bit product of two odd 1,024-bit integers, its upper half and remainder modulo 120 identify 121 sums worth comparing. One fits at least as many compatible integer pairs as any other sum.
scope: This ranks possible sums. The rule missed both 2,048-bit comparison products.
detail: Among 228,713 products of two 14-bit primes, ranking guessed correctly on 64,531. Ordinary Fermat search with the same remainder got 57,568 on its first guess and 192,183 with the ranking’s total square-root budget. Every successful ranked guess was covered at that budget.

title: One sum survives 52 candidates
impact: The surviving sum, 5,474, gives 2,293 × 3,181 from the product and the 12-bit factor width.
scope: One 23-bit product. Using the exact interval still left both 2,048-bit comparison products unfactored.
detail: The width bounds give 52 positions. Four pass the test modulo 63, and only one passes modulo 315. Constructing the table and its period takes 316 greatest-common-divisor calculations and 144 modular inversions before the final square test.

title: Two guesses find the most common sum among odd factor pairs
impact: Knowing only the upper half of the product bits, two row counts suffice to identify a sum shared by the most odd factor pairs.
scope: Proved for equal factor widths of at least 14 bits, including 1,024. The most common sum among prime pairs can be different.
detail: On 228,713 products of two 14-bit primes, ranking odd pairs gave 14,926 correct guesses. The first ordinary Fermat midpoint gave 17,324. The new rule found 83 that Fermat missed and missed 2,481 that Fermat found. Neither full-size control split.

title: Three quarters of the product bits still leave the sum hard to guess
impact: Even a list of 2⁴⁰ sums can cover fewer than one in 2⁴³⁴ eligible prime pairs if it sees only the top 1,024 bits and the bottom 512 bits.
scope: Uniformly chosen pairs of distinct 1,024-bit primes with a 2,048-bit product. A method using its middle 512 bits can use information outside this bound.
detail: Giving the rule the exact square-root ceiling, width quotients and remainder modulo 24 as well still keeps coverage below one in 2⁴²⁶. The proof counts pairs by how many times their difference can be divided by two.

title: Skipping multiples that cannot reveal the factors
impact: The product rules out at least 81% of the multiples in one complete difference-of-squares search.
scope: Every eligible 2,048-bit product still has more than 10¹⁰² qualifying multiples. A bounded trial on the fresh example fell from 11,328 square tests to 851 and missed.
detail: In one complete search for two unknown 1,024-bit primes with a 2,048-bit product, we can skip at least 81% of the trial multiples. More than 10¹⁰² different multiples still qualify on every such input. On our fresh example, the shorter search used 851 exact square tests down from 11,328 over the same bounded range. Both searches missed.

sources.label: How the product rules out multiples

title: The same interval can fit many different prime sums
impact: For all but fewer than one pair in a billion, more than 2⁹⁰⁰ true sums occur among products that share the recorded data.
scope: Distinct 1,024-bit primes with a 2,048-bit product. The record includes the upper 1,024 product bits, the square-root ceiling, two quotients and the remainder modulo 24.
detail: Even a separately supplied 128-bit hint and a trillion candidate sums (up to 2⁴⁰) cover fewer than one in 2³⁹⁶ eligible pairs under this information model. An algorithm using other digits of the product to choose guesses falls outside the bound.

title: Three equations that cover every pair of primes above three
impact: At least one equation has a pair of solutions that reveals the factors. A bounded search split 22 of 32 fresh 40-bit inputs.
scope: For any two distinct primes above three. Locating the solutions still costs work. Five of 32 fresh 48-bit inputs split and both full-size comparisons remained unresolved.
detail: We can give three equations for any product of two different primes above three. One equation has solutions that reveal the factors. Finding them remains hard. The search split 22 of 32 fresh 40-bit numbers and five of 32 at 48 bits. Both 2,048-bit comparisons stayed unresolved.

title: At most one square test per proposed power
impact: The new stopping rule kept all 130 small factorizations while reducing square roots from 16,287 to 797.
scope: Across 12,994 small products with equal-width primes. The separate full-size trials found no factor.
detail: One square-root test per guess suffices for a search using continued fractions. Across 12,994 small products it kept all 130 factorizations and cut 16,287 square roots to 797. A separate run tried 106 guesses large enough to pass the division test on each of two 2,048-bit products and found neither pair.

title: When the first guess at the sum is enough
impact: The first even sum at or above twice the square root works on more than one in 2⁵¹⁷ eligible prime pairs.
scope: A guaranteed lower bound across the full 2,048-bit population. Close primes supply the successes, and the bound is too small to predict success on an individual input.
detail: The method tries even sums in increasing order. Counting primes that fall in the same short interval proves a success rate without assuming a random distribution of primes inside each short interval.

title: Two possible sums from 45 guesses
impact: A remainder test left 2,746 and 2,854 for 1,879,513. The second sum gave 1,031 × 1,823.
scope: A 45-position window on one small input. At full size, sums 20,160 apart can both pass somewhere at every modulus.
detail: Two guesses out of 45 survived the remainder tests for 1,879,513. The second gave 1,031 × 1,823. At 2,048 bits we proved a limit on the same idea. For every product, two guesses 20,160 apart can both pass somewhere, whatever modulus we choose.

title: Which extra fractions are worth checking?
impact: Including intermediate fractions found 118 of 903 small products, up from 78.
scope: All distinct pairs of 9-bit primes. On two 2,048-bit inputs, 106 guesses narrowed to 9 and 33 fractions without revealing a factor.
detail: A wider search found 118 of 903 small prime pairs, including 40 missed by the earlier version. It narrowed 106 guesses on each of two 2,048-bit products to 9 and 33 candidate fractions. Neither yielded a factor.

title: When adding a small number reveals the prime sum
impact: Trying 64 neighbors recovered 466 of 903 small products. Adding four to 108,671 gave the clue for 271 × 401.
scope: Even granting every divisor of the neighbors, this rule covers fewer than one in 2⁹⁷⁶ eligible 2,048-bit products.
detail: Adding four to 108,671 exposes a divisor that predicts the prime sum 672 and gives 271 × 401. Trying 64 nearby integers this way found 466 of 903 small products. At full size, even with every divisor available, fewer than one in 2⁹⁷⁶ eligible products can be recovered by that rule.

title: How often small prime powers can reveal the sum
impact: Exhausting the permitted powers can recover fewer than one in 2⁵⁵³ eligible 2,048-bit products.
scope: Applies to this continued-fraction rule, with exponents no greater than the product and all prime divisors at most 1,500.
detail: Could making more guesses find the two primes? For one method, suppose we try every number whose prime factors are all at most 1,500, stopping at the input number. This can recover the pair for fewer than one in 2⁵⁵³ balanced 2,048-bit products.

title: What an effective choice of exponent would reveal
impact: One exponent made a comparison succeed on three sevenths of the starting values for a 2,048-bit example.
scope: That exponent was chosen with the known factors. Five exponents chosen from the product gave no practical improvement.
detail: One power chosen with the known primes made a small set of comparisons succeed three times in seven on a 2,048-bit example. The proof explains what choosing such a power would require. Five powers computed from the product gave no practical improvement on this example.

title: Can a different starting value rescue a power comparison?
impact: On two 2,048-bit products, no starting value let cross-row comparisons find an additional factor.
scope: The proof used the published primes to check every starting value for this bounded comparison after its preliminary tests.
detail: Could a different starting number rescue a failed search? On two 2,048-bit examples we checked every possible starting number for one bounded search. Comparing powers across different rows could never add a factor after the preliminary checks. We used the known primes to establish that limit.

title: How far the multiplier search must go
impact: Only two multipliers work on each comparison product. The search passes at least 2⁵⁰¹ eligible multipliers before its first hit.
scope: Retrospective check using the published factors of two 2,048-bit products.
detail: We used the published factors to check exactly where one search would succeed on our two 2,048-bit examples. Only two multiples work on each input. Starting at one, the search must pass at least 2⁵⁰¹ eligible multiples before reaching the first answer.

detail: A shorter sieve period let us fit two entire smaller searches within their budgets. Lean also verified four fresh 96-bit products under the same budgets. On one, only the shorter period guaranteed full coverage, but a full-period competitor found the actual answer sooner. This lookup exceeded the budget on both 2,048-bit comparisons.

title: Choosing a table that fits in memory
impact: A new split let the search store 20,000 entries and test its first three rows on each full-size control.
scope: Neither three-row scan found a factor. Each full search still had more than 2⁸⁸⁰ rows.
detail: With a different table split, 20,000 entries let the search start on both full-size inputs. We visited three rows on each and found no factors. More than 2⁸⁸⁰ rows remained in each scan.

title: Storing one entry for two possible sums
impact: Pairing entries halved the table to 18,711 entries on a 92-bit product and 17,820 on a 91-bit product. Both searches found the factors.
scope: For the same layout on the full-size controls, even one byte per required entry exceeds 10¹³⁴ bytes.
detail: Pairing search entries halved the memory on two small test products. We recovered both primes of a 92-bit number with 18,711 stored entries, and a 91-bit number with 17,820. Lean checked both answers. At 2,048 bits even one byte per required entry would exceed 10¹³⁴ bytes.

title: Discarding impossible sums before building a polynomial
impact: Filtering the candidate sums let a fresh 66-bit search finish within budget. It found 6,860,100,517 and 7,585,863,317.
scope: On both 2,048-bit controls the resulting polynomial still required more than 2⁵⁰⁷ coefficients.
detail: A fresh 66-bit product gave the primes 6,860,100,517 and 7,585,863,317 in 0.69 seconds. Filtering out impossible sums kept the search inside its budget. The same filter still required a polynomial with more than 2⁵⁰⁷ coefficients on each 2,048-bit comparison.

title: Finding the position shared by repeated matches
impact: Several positions matched modulo each prime of 30,607. A more precise reading recovered their shared position and the factors 127 and 241.
scope: The calculation uses the product. Its success here depends on resolving the repeated matches within the available precision.
detail: On 30,607, several positions matched at each prime. A more precise reading picked out their shared position and recovered 127 × 241.

title: Reusing powers when checking possible sums
impact: On a fresh 88-bit input, reusing powers cut 92,665 modular exponentiations to 98 and recovered both primes.
scope: On a constructed 2,048-bit example, the published factors certify that base 2 distinguishes the sum. Searching for it still exceeded budget.
detail: Base 2 uniquely identifies the correct sum on our independently constructed 2,048-bit example. Lean checked that fact using the published factors. Finding the sum still exceeded the full-size search budget. On a fresh 88-bit product, reusing powers cut 92,665 modular exponentiations to 98 and recovered both primes.

title: Two remainder checks identify one sum in 15,902
impact: Two checks picked the correct sum on a fresh 52-bit product, yielding 52,902,449 and 55,986,167.
scope: On each 2,048-bit control the planned search tables exceeded 2⁴⁴⁹ entries.
detail: Two modular checks picked the right sum out of 15,902 candidates on a fresh 52-bit product. The sum gave 52,902,449 × 55,986,167. On the 2,048-bit examples, the search tables would have needed more than 2⁴⁴⁹ entries.

sources.label: Limits of predicting from product digits

title: Choosing a number base from a neighbor of the product
impact: A base dividing 135,137 minus one exposed 337 and 401 after ten remainder checks.
scope: Every power-of-two base in the same range missed this example within the specified lower correction range.
detail: Subtracting one from 135,137 helped us choose the base that revealed 337 × 401. Every comparable power of two missed. We checked when choosing the base this way could work at 2,048 bits.

sources.label: How the product selects the base

title: Testing a whole range of carry guesses
impact: Two square tests and one gcd recovered a constructed 2,048-bit pair despite a 354-bit correction to the initial guess.
scope: An earlier method also solved this constructed input. Both previous full-size controls survived the new search.
detail: Two square tests found the primes of a specially constructed 2,048-bit product, even with a 354-bit error in our initial guess. A previous method also solved this example. Most ranges on two earlier products remain unresolved.

title: Recovering two constructed products from their digits
impact: A carry pattern revealed both primes in two 2,048-bit products after 129 and 996 square-root tests.
scope: The primes were chosen to produce the pattern. Two earlier products each survived 41,472 guesses.
detail: A pattern in the binary digits gave away both primes in two constructed 2,048-bit products. The searches took 129 and 996 square-root tests. Two earlier products of the same size each survived 41,472 guesses.

sources.label: Try it on 143 and see how rare the pattern is

title: A wrong sum can still expose a factor
impact: Guessing 366 for the sum of the factors of 33,017 exposed 241. The correct sum was 378.
scope: Even allowing over four million bases, the bounded search covers fewer than one in 2⁴⁴ eligible 2,048-bit pairs.
detail: A wrong guess found 137 × 241. On 33,017 the program tried a sum of 366. The correct sum is 378, yet the calculation revealed 241. Even trying over four million bases, this bounded search could find a match on fewer than one in 17.5 trillion randomly chosen target pairs.

title: Reusing four plans for twelve products
impact: Four reusable plans recovered all twelve fresh 27-digit products in 11.70 seconds including preparation. Building a plan per product took 11.96 seconds.
scope: These local timings include setup and execution on 88-bit and 89-bit inputs.
detail: Four reusable search plans found both primes of twelve new 27-digit products. Including the time to make all four plans, this took about 11.70 seconds in our comparison. Making a fresh plan for each product took about 11.96 seconds.

title: Finding the fewest blocks for a fixed search
impact: For one 89-bit product the optimal schedule used 33,010 blocks, down from 34,264. A proof rules out a shorter complete schedule with the same weights and table size.
scope: Planning took 155 seconds and execution about one second. The full-size controls remained beyond budget.
detail: On an 89-bit product we recovered both primes with 33,010 search blocks. The previous planner used 34,264. A matching lower bound proves the new schedule is the cheapest for those weights and table size. Finding the plan took 155 seconds and executing it took about one second. This weighted search still exceeds the budget on both full-size comparisons.

title: Recovering primes from a nearby predictable sum
impact: Four polynomial calculations recovered the factors of a constructed 2,048-bit product even though the sum missed its prediction by a 121-digit integer.
scope: The primes were chosen near a sum made from powers of two and three. At the same tolerance, both earlier full-size controls provably miss.
detail: We chose two 1,024-bit primes whose sum was close to a predictable number. Even though our guess was off by a 121-digit number, four polynomial calculations recovered both primes from their product. On two earlier inputs Lean proved the same shortcut could never find the factors at that tolerance.

sources.label: Why it works and how rare it is

title: When the factor sum uses only twos and threes
impact: Given the product alone, 26 square tests recovered both primes of a constructed 2,048-bit input.
scope: The method covers every target pair with this sum pattern. Fewer than one in 2⁹⁹⁸ eligible pairs can have it.
detail: We recovered both primes of a constructed 2,048-bit product in 26 square tests. We chose the primes so their sum used only powers of 2 and 3. Given only the product, the search works for every pair with that pattern. Fewer than one pair in 2⁹⁹⁸ at the target size can have it. The two earlier controls both rule it out.

title: Looking for a sum with only small prime divisors
impact: A check on the product plus one recovered a constructed 43-bit pair using 19 remainder checks and one square test.
scope: Both 2,048-bit controls missed. Sums built only from primes up to 31 occur for fewer than one in 2⁹⁴⁷ eligible pairs.
detail: A calculation on the product plus one found 2,101,249 × 3,658,751 on a constructed 43-bit example. It took 19 remainder checks and one square test. Both 2,048-bit controls missed. When the proposed sum uses only primes through 31, the method covers less than one in 2⁹⁴⁷ of the target products, even with the best guess for each input.

title: How many straight lines can represent a division table?
impact: Changes in two division tables give the smaller prime exactly. Even the best straight-line representation needed 3,700 pieces on a 46-bit input.
scope: The particular representation needs more than 2⁵⁰⁷ pieces on each full-size control.
detail: Adding the changes in two division tables gives the smaller prime exactly. We tested how much those tables shrink when represented by straight-line pieces. One 46-bit example needed 3,700 pieces. Both large examples provably need more than 2⁵⁰⁷ pieces.

sources.label: Formula and limits of this calculation

title: Selecting one factor interval by an equation
impact: One equation selected interval 26 of 37 on 101,000,651 and led to 10,007 and 10,093.
scope: The possible sum was already fixed within this example’s interval. Fermat’s first square test found the same factors.
detail: One equation selected range 26 of 37 on 101,000,651, giving 10,007 × 10,093. The primes in this example are close enough for Fermat’s first square test to succeed. We still need to construct a useful equation in the range number for other products.

title: The best single random divisor guess
impact: If smaller positive guesses are at least as likely as larger ones, even the best single gcd draw succeeds with probability below 2⁻¹⁰²² for two distinct 1,024-bit primes.
scope: This bound covers every distribution with that ordering. For 77 the exact optimum is 13 in 56.
detail: Can random guesses help locate a prime? If smaller positive integers are at least as likely as larger ones, even the best distribution gives less than one chance in 2¹⁰²² per guess of finding a proper factor at the target size. For 77 the exact best chance is 13 in 56.

title: Rounding smaller equations cuts the number of intervals
impact: With the same number of coefficients per equation, each full-size control needed less than a third of the previous number of locations.
scope: Lean checked the coverage counts. Both complete lists still exceed 10¹⁴⁸ locations.
detail: The complete list of ranges on each large example is less than one third as long as before. Each list still has more than 10¹⁴⁸ entries. Lean proved those counts without running the full search.

sources.label: Work per range and full counts

title: Seven coefficients rule out wider intervals
impact: Rounding a sifted equation excluded intervals three times and twice as wide on the two 2,048-bit controls. On 132,079 the method found 269 and 491.
scope: The searches used the products and public centers. Neither chosen full-size interval yielded a factor.
detail: In the tests we ran, seven coefficients gave 269 × 491 = 132,079 on the small example. On the two large inputs, the same method ruled out ranges three times and twice as wide as before. The project knows the two prime pairs from construction. These searches received only the products and recovered neither pair.

title: One equation covers 5,359 original intervals
impact: Using whole-number positions lets one equation handle 5,359 stretches of the original grid at the same row count.
scope: Two small equations excluded selected intervals. Full coverage on the 2,048-bit controls still costs roughly 2⁴⁹⁵ and 2⁴⁹⁶ locations with larger equations.
detail: By using whole-number positions, one equation now covers 5,359 of our original ranges. Two small equations ruled out their chosen ranges on the 2,048-bit examples. A full search still needs roughly 2⁴⁹⁵ and 2⁴⁹⁶ locations, with much larger equations.

sources.label: Factor example, proof and full-size limits

title: Testing two neighboring intervals together
impact: One equation covers two adjacent stretches and recovered 269 × 491 on 132,079 where the previous bound missed.
scope: Each full-size comparison still requires more than 2⁵⁰⁶ locations.
detail: One equation now checks two neighboring ranges. On 132,079, this gave 269 × 491 where the previous bound missed. Even with this change, the full search on each 2,048-bit comparison needs more than 2⁵⁰⁶ locations.

title: Two product measurements determine the factor sum
impact: The readings on 143 gave the sum 24, which recovers 11 and 13.
scope: Both measurements use the public product. Computing them took more work than ordinary search on the larger examples timed.
detail: Two measurements of a product also give the exact sum of the hidden primes. On 143 the readings gave 24, which yields 11 and 13. Computing the readings took more work than an ordinary search on the larger examples we timed.

title: Narrowing the smaller prime’s range from the product
impact: Using the actual product to bound both endpoints and the interval widths covers the smaller factor in fewer than 2⁵⁰⁹ locations.
scope: The full bound for two 1,024-bit primes requires 24,576 rows at each location.
detail: Using the actual product narrows the possible range for the smaller prime. Lean proves that two window sizes cover it in fewer than 2⁵⁰⁹ locations. The construction requires 24,576 rows at each location and remains beyond practical reach.

title: A higher-degree equation checks a wider interval
impact: At a chosen location a degree-eight equation checks about 70 trillion times as many possible odd factors as the earlier degree-four equation.
scope: Both chosen 2,048-bit intervals were empty. The result prices coverage at a location and leaves the choice of location open.
detail: A degree-eight equation checked about 70 trillion times as many possible odd factors at a chosen location as our previous quartic. Both 2,048-bit intervals we tried were empty.

title: Three equations expose a shared divisor
impact: On 22,663, combining three equations exposed the divisor 173 and yielded 131 × 173.
scope: The five checks of the earlier method all missed on the same interval of eleven odd candidates.
detail: Starting with 22,663, three equations gave a number sharing the factor 173 with the input. The other prime was 131. In the same interval, all five checks from the previous method missed.

title: A determinant reveals the square of a prime
impact: Four equations gave a multiple of the input whose quotient was 28,141,469 squared, revealing a prime on a 49-bit product.
scope: One of 4,827 search windows split that product. Five windows on each full-size control yielded no factor.
detail: Four equations in our 49-bit search produced the input times the exact square of one prime. A square root gave 28,141,469. Only one of 4,827 windows gave a split. Five windows per 2,048-bit example yielded none.

title: Testing a chosen factor interval with one equation
impact: One quartic checks 2⁴⁰⁸ + 1 nearby odd candidates for a 1,024-bit factor. It recovered 41 and 61 on a small example.
scope: The chosen intervals were empty on both 2,048-bit controls. Complete coverage can require 2⁶¹⁴ equations.
detail: At any chosen odd location, one equation now checks 2⁴⁰⁸ + 1 odd candidates for a 1,024-bit factor. Lean ruled out the chosen interval on both 2,048-bit examples. A complete search can still take 2⁶¹⁴ equations. On 2,501 the same rule returned 41 × 61.

title: Reusing the equation from a neighboring interval
impact: Reusing the previous basis cut a complete 49-bit search from 1.275 to 0.642 CPU seconds and recovered both primes.
scope: Only five neighboring intervals were tested on each 2,048-bit product.
detail: Reusing the previous interval’s calculation cut a complete 49-bit search from 1.275 to 0.642 CPU seconds. It found 17,838,631 × 28,141,469. We tried five neighboring intervals on each 2,048-bit example. Both searches still have most intervals left to visit.

title: Combining blocks with the same factor coordinate
impact: On a 49-bit product, grouping blocks cut 2,884 calculations to 914 and retained the factorization.
scope: One calculation represented the last 2²⁵⁷ blocks on a 2,048-bit example. Three positions were tested without a factor.
detail: One calculation covered the last 2²⁵⁷ blocks of possible smaller factors on a 2,048-bit example. Any factor in that stretch would use the same row of the search. We tried three positions and found no factor. On a 49-bit example, combining blocks cut 2,884 calculations to 914 and recovered both primes.

title: Counting a complete list of factor tests
impact: For every pair of distinct 1,024-bit primes, a list of fewer than 2⁶⁹² tests determined by their product contains a prime factor.
scope: Merely enumerating its groups takes at least 2⁵⁰³ visits on each of the two full-size controls.
detail: For any two distinct 1,024-bit primes, the product determines a list of fewer than 2⁶⁹² tests containing a prime factor. Lean proves the guarantee. On each of our two full-size examples, exhaustively listing the groups for this method already takes at least 2⁵⁰³ visits. We still need a way to pick the right group quickly. The search found 556,587,319 × 584,628,763 on a fresh 59-bit input.

title: Subdividing the curve of possible factors
impact: Across four groups on each full-size input, fewer than 2¹⁷⁵ tests cover more than 2⁴⁹² positions.
scope: Even those groups require more than 2¹⁷³ pieces. The first three pieces tested per input yielded no factor.
detail: A short part of the factor curve can be checked with one equation per sign. On each of two 2,048-bit inputs, four groups that held more than 2⁴⁹² candidate positions can now be covered in fewer than 2¹⁷⁵ tests. Even those four groups require more than 2¹⁷³ pieces with this method. We counted them and tested three pieces per input. Neither run found a factor. The same approach found 17,838,631 × 28,141,469 on the smaller example.

title: Keeping digits forced by remainders
impact: Forced digits cut the exhaustive 49-bit search from 4,800 groups to 3,040.
scope: Each of the two 2,048-bit schedules still contains more than 2⁸⁸⁸ groups.
detail: A remainder can force another digit of the answer during the lattice search. Keeping those digits cut the exhaustive 49-bit example from 4,800 groups to 3,040. The fresh and crossed 2,048-bit schedules still exceed 2⁸⁸⁸ groups each.

sources.label: What knowing the coordinates would tell us

title: Grouping divisor tests by remainder
impact: A complete 49-bit search fell from 7.39 seconds to 0.59 seconds and recovered 17,838,631 and 28,141,469.
scope: Eight groups tested on each of two 2,048-bit controls yielded no factor.
detail: We found the primes 17,838,631 and 28,141,469 by grouping the tests for their product, 502,005,281,288,939. Searching 4,800 groups took 0.59 seconds, down from 7.39 seconds for the previous complete remainder search. Eight groups apiece on two 2,048-bit inputs yielded no factors.

sources.label: Why grouping works and how much remains

title: Skipping square tests using small prime remainders
impact: On 134,683,853, remainder checks cut 4,710 square tests to 156 and retained both factors.
scope: Computing the jumps took longer. The proof leaves more than 2⁸⁹³ combinations for every permitted choice of small primes at full size.
detail: Dividing the product by small primes gives remainders we can use to skip impossible tests. On 134,683,853 this cut 4,710 square tests to 156 and recovered 8,231 and 16,363, though computing the jumps cost more time. The proof covers every 2,048-bit product of two distinct 1,024-bit primes. Our two full-size examples still have about 2⁸⁹⁹ combinations to search. The first 64 yielded no factor on either. Lean also proves that any choice of distinct odd primes satisfying this method’s size requirement leaves more than 2⁸⁹³ combinations.

title: How far away the winning adjustments can be
impact: The complete offset search has exactly one or two successful positions.
scope: Its first trillion adjustments reach fewer than one in 2⁴²² random balanced target-size pairs.
detail: The original search range always contains exactly one or two winning positions. Even the first trillion adjustments can reach fewer than one in 2⁴²² random prime pairs of the target size.

sources.label: Why there are at most two

title: A product-selected square test
impact: One square test recovered both factors of two specially constructed 2,048-bit products.
scope: It missed both comparison inputs. Even all multipliers in the family cover fewer than one in 2⁴⁸¹ balanced prime pairs at that size.
detail: One rule lets the product select a single square test. It recovered both primes on two constructed 2,048-bit numbers and missed on both earlier comparison numbers. Even testing every multiplier in this family covers fewer than one in 2⁴⁸¹ balanced prime pairs at this size.

title: A product-selected filter for square tests
impact: On the fresh 2,048-bit input, the filter reduced about 42 billion survivors to 19 billion among a trillion choices.
scope: Testing 64 survivors per version found no full-size factor. A smaller example split at adjustment 13.
detail: A broader square test found 36,559 × 64,997 at adjustment 13. On the fresh 2,048-bit number, selecting the filter from the product cut the survivors from roughly 42 billion to 19 billion out of a trillion choices. Testing 64 survivors in each version yielded no factor.

title: Using the factor sum to remove groups
impact: The sum bounds reduced the number of groups fourfold on the fresh 2,048-bit product. A later test excluded 2,048 groups together in 0.76 seconds.
scope: These exclusions left both full-size factors unknown to the search.
detail: On the fresh 2,048-bit example, using the possible sums of the two primes cut the number of groups to search by a factor of four. A later test ruled out 2,048 of those groups together in 0.76 seconds. This search has not recovered either of the two primes used to build the example.

sources.label: Fresh result, Lean exclusion proof and remaining work

title: Testing a guess for one factor remainder
impact: A single guess recovered the two 1,024-bit primes of the crossed control in 2.21 seconds.
scope: The original guess used the published factors. Fixed in advance, it succeeded on three of ten constructed inputs and missed a fresh product.
detail: One guess recovered both 1,024-bit primes of our earlier comparison number in 2.21 seconds. We chose it after seeing the published factors. Testing the same guess using only the products succeeded on three of ten constructed examples and missed the other seven. It also missed a fresh product generated after we fixed the guess.

sources.label: See the two primes and Lean certificate

title: Checking four groups with one equation
impact: In a successful group the equation leaves at most four possible factors. Finite differences cut the complete count by another 43% in a matched comparison.
scope: The count of groups on the fresh 2,048-bit input still has 184 decimal digits.
detail: One equation now checks four of the original groups at once. If we choose the right group, it leaves at most four possible factors. On our 2,048-bit test number, using these equations cut the number of groups by a factor of about 64 quintillion compared with our earlier linear search. Checking positive and negative solutions together almost halved the count again. Using finite differences cut the complete count a further 43% in a matched comparison. On the fresh product, using the difference between the factors cut another 29% compared with ordinary Newton equations. The number of groups still has 184 digits.

sources.label: How finite differences reduce the search

title: One weighted sum for a group of factor pairs
impact: Complete searches on eight fresh 49–50-bit inputs took 0.058 seconds in total, compared with 1.003 seconds for trial division in the same intervals.
scope: At 2,048 bits a complete search still requires more than 2⁶⁷⁶ groups.
detail: One weighted sum can check an entire group of factor pairs. On 34,387, four groups led to a single sum and the factors 137 and 251. Across eight fresh 49–50-bit inputs, the complete search took 0.058 seconds, compared with 1.003 seconds for trial division over the same intervals. A complete search by this rule still needs more than 2⁶⁷⁶ groups at 2,048 bits.

sources.label: Grouping related checks on an 82-bit input

title: Choosing a base to reduce candidate pairs
impact: Changing the base cut the number of pairs checked from 4,478 to 1,853 across eight fresh inputs. Both searches recovered every pair.
scope: Trial division was faster on all eight, and the 2,048-bit search still exceeds 2⁶⁸⁰ groups.
detail: Changing the base used to write the two unknown factors cut the candidate pairs checked from 4,478 to 1,853 across eight fresh products. Both searches found every pair. Ordinary trial division was faster on all eight inputs. At 2,048 bits the new search would still visit more than 2⁶⁸⁰ groups.

title: Wrong midpoints that survive prime-power tests
impact: For every target-size product, more than 2⁸⁷⁴ wrong midpoints survive all powers of all primes through 733.
scope: Local tests can isolate the answer on small inputs. Powers of 2, 3 and 5 isolated the midpoint for 34,387.
detail: On 34,387, tests at powers of 2, 3 and 5 left exactly one possible midpoint for the primes. It gave 137 and 251. On our 2,048-bit comparison input, three prime-power tests eliminated 99.126% of the interval and still left a 1,013-bit count of possibilities. Even at every power of every prime through 733, more than 2⁸⁷⁴ wrong midpoints survive on every target-size product.

title: Narrower intervals for weighted sums
impact: On one 89-bit product the search fell from 14.18 to 1.34 seconds. It also factored a fresh 99-bit product in 7.59 seconds.
scope: GNU factor took 0.325 seconds on the 99-bit input. A full 2,048-bit search needs more than 2⁴⁰⁴ records.
detail: Narrowing the possible sums of two weighted factors recovered both primes of a fresh 99-bit number in 7.59 seconds. GNU’s factor utility took 0.325 seconds on that number. On the same 89-bit input, the previous full-interval search took 14.18 seconds and this search took 1.34 seconds. On the 2,048-bit control, 96 blocks yielded no factor. A full search with these windows would need more than 2⁴⁰⁴ records.

title: Reading a prime as a sum of squares
impact: Two character sums can encode a prime as a sum of squares. On 26,441 the readings gave 11 and 4, recovering 137.
scope: Both primes must be 1 modulo 4 for this result. The example required 26,440 symbol evaluations.
detail: For products whose primes both leave remainder 1 when divided by 4, two sums encode a prime as a sum of two squares. On 26,441 we recovered 11 and 4, whose squares add to 137. Calculating the two sums still took 26,440 symbol evaluations.

title: Recovering a factor from a sum over pairs
impact: On 77 a sum over pairs equals 21. Adding one and dividing by two gives the prime 11 even though both ordinary sums vanish.
scope: Directly evaluating the pair sum took 5,929 positions on this small input.
detail: Both ordinary sums vanish on 77. A sum over pairs gives 21, so (21 + 1) / 2 recovers 11. The same approach extends to other prime pairs. Computing the sum directly on 77 took 5,929 positions.

sources.label: Why the formula works and how the cost grows

title: Charging the cost of filtering possible divisors
impact: Remainder compatibility reduced 83,891 possible divisors to 16,908 on a 41-bit input.
scope: The complete search took eight times longer once it included the work of applying the filter.
detail: On a 41-bit input, checking whether candidate factors have compatible remainders cut 83,891 possible divisors to 16,908. The complete search took eight times longer once we counted the work of excluding candidates.

title: Three expressions for the smaller prime
impact: For any two distinct odd primes, one of three expressions yields the smaller one. On 713 a final gcd gives 23.
scope: Computing that gcd's input is expensive. With two 1,024-bit primes, searching both coordinates only up to 2⁵¹⁰ cannot succeed.
detail: For any product of two distinct odd primes, one of three simple expressions equals its smaller prime. On 713 our formula returns 23 in one greatest common divisor calculation. The work goes into the product used in that calculation. For two 1,024-bit primes, checking even the full range up to 2⁵¹⁰ in both coordinates finds nothing.

title: A smaller-coordinate search against direct division
impact: The search recovered 2,423,330,473 and 2,513,756,873 on a fresh 63-bit product.
scope: Searching the possible odd divisors directly was faster on the same input.
detail: On a fresh 63-bit input, the smaller-coordinate search found 2,423,330,473 and 2,513,756,873. A direct search of the possible odd divisors was faster on this input.

title: How often weighted sums of squares reveal factors
impact: At most 132 weights and 849 multiples per weight suffice to contain two revealing solutions for all but fewer than one in 2¹¹⁹ of the specified prime pairs.
scope: The probability is over uniform distinct 1,024-bit primes with a 2,048-bit product. The full-size comparison exhausted its budget searching for the solutions.
detail: From a 2,048-bit product we can select at most 132 weights for a sum of two squares and try up to 849 multiples of the product per weight. For two uniformly chosen distinct 1,024-bit primes giving a product of this size, fewer than one pair in 2¹¹⁹ lacks two revealing solutions in this search. Finding those solutions is still expensive. On a small example we started with 3,599 and found 59 and 61. Our 2,048-bit comparison exhausted its search budget.

title: Changing the polynomial during a search
impact: At the same search budget, changing polynomials factored six of 16 fresh 79-bit products. One ordinary interval found no factors.
scope: The comparison measures this fixed sample and budget.
detail: On the same 16 fresh 79-bit products, one ordinary interval found no factors at its fixed budget. Changing the polynomial at regular intervals found both primes on six inputs.

title: Finding factors from short fractions
impact: Checking 24 multiples recovered both primes of a 2,048-bit product constructed to have a short usable fraction.
scope: On the second full-size product 57,769 square roots exhausted the reduced search. Every successful pair of fractions was outside its range.
detail: We found both primes of a specially constructed 2,048-bit number after checking 24 of its multiples. On a second number of the same size, a faster search cut over two million square roots to 57,769 and exhausted its range. We proved that every working pair of fractions on this second number exceeds that range.

title: The chance of drawing two useful fractions together
impact: Two fractions from the same draw split 77,837 on the seventeenth try.
scope: For a target-size product, even 281 trillion random tries have probability below 2⁻⁷⁴⁸ of producing the required pair under the stated sampling rule.
detail: Two fractions from the same draw can guarantee a factor. Our search found such a pair for 77,837 on its seventeenth try and recovered 277 and 281. For a 2,048-bit product of two 1,024-bit primes, even 281 trillion random tries have less chance of producing such a pair than 748 fair coins have of all landing heads.

sources.label: See the example and sampling assumptions

title: Trading more fraction checks for fewer draws
impact: Trying all proportions recovered a sampled 79-bit product in 70,166 draws, down from 1,211,456.
scope: Testing more fractions per draw increased the total CPU time on that input.
detail: Writing a square remainder as a fraction split a sampled 79-bit product. Trying all proportions needed 70,166 draws, down from 1,211,456. Checking more fractions took more CPU time on this input. At 2,048 bits we can bound how rarely these searches yield a usable row.

title: Scoring continued-fraction multipliers from the product
impact: At a fixed step limit, a product-based multiplier choice raised successes from 14 to 26 among 64 fresh 79-bit products.
scope: The comparison establishes a gain on those small products. The score can miss useful multipliers at 2,048 bits.
detail: Using the product to choose a starting multiplier improved a continued-fraction search on a fresh sample. It found both primes in 26 of 64 cases, up from 14 at the same step limit. All the products in that comparison had 79 bits.

sources.label: Why the score can fail at 2,048 bits

title: Combining small remainders across a fresh sample
impact: Combining remainders split 13 of 64 fresh 79-bit products. Continued fractions split 15, with 12 successes in common.
scope: On a 2,048-bit product more than four billion classes gave 58 small remainders. None of their combinations revealed a factor.
detail: On 64 fresh 79-bit products, combining small remainders recovered both primes in 13 cases. Continued fractions succeeded in 15, with 12 successes in common. On a 2,048-bit test, we searched more than four billion possible classes and found 58 small remainders. No combination of those 58 gave a factor.

title: A full-size split from related prime orders
impact: A search given only the product recovered both primes on its thirteenth try in a constructed 2,048-bit example.
scope: One prime plus one divided the other prime squared minus one. After replacing one prime, the same thirteen tries found nothing.
detail: We built a 2,048-bit example where one prime plus one divides the other prime squared minus one. A search given only the product found both primes on its thirteenth try. We then replaced just one prime. The product was still 2,048 bits, and the same thirteen tries found nothing.

title: Grouping quotient intervals by residue modulo six
impact: Grouping the balanced interval for 1,900,014,700,027 cut the search from 5,111 strips to 1,708 and recovered 1,000,003 and 1,900,009.
scope: This is a complete comparison on one small product. The method still searches multiple strips.
detail: A search of the full balanced range for 1,900,014,700,027 took 1,708 strips when we grouped factors by their remainders modulo 6, down from 5,111. It recovered the primes 1,000,003 and 1,900,009. On 77,837, three unsuccessful divisor checks together revealed 277 and 281.

title: Recognizing the correct midpoint with random checks
impact: Among distinct 1,024-bit primes with a 2,048-bit product, 1,040 random checks identify the midpoint with probability above 99.9999% when every candidate is tested.
scope: The checks still require a candidate search. The 41-bit example tested all 41,807 possibilities.
detail: For two distinct 1,024-bit primes with a 2,048-bit product, 1,040 random checks can identify their average with over 99.9999% probability if we test every candidate. On a 41-bit example, we tested all 41,807 candidates to find the one that passed.

title: A binomial remainder that gives the larger prime
impact: For odd primes p < q < 4p, a binomial remainder determined by their product gives the larger prime exactly.
scope: This covers any two distinct 1,024-bit primes. Direct evaluation already needed a 761,262-bit intermediate on a 31-bit product. Efficient full-size evaluation remains open.
detail: For 143 = 11 × 13, the chosen coefficient leaves remainder 12, revealing the larger prime 13. The ratio condition q < 4p is essential to the stated guarantee.

title: Recovering the factors from one rounded value
impact: On 32 full-size products a value accurate to 1,366 fractional bits gave both primes with one square test.
scope: Known primes supplied the full-size values. A smaller value was computed directly for 60,491, recovering 241 and 251.
detail: On 32 full-size products, one value rounded to 1,366 fractional bits let us recover both primes with one square test. We used known primes to generate each value. We also computed a shorter value directly from 60,491 and recovered 241 and 251. Finding a cheap way to compute it at full size remains open.

sources.label: How many bits suffice on average?

title: When a continued fraction reveals a planted relation
impact: Removing a multiplier revealed both factors of a constructed 2,048-bit product in four steps.
scope: The input had a close match between small multiples of its primes. A multiplier of 133 exhausted 65,536 steps on the same number.
detail: On the same specially constructed 2,048-bit product, a search using a multiplier of 133 exhausted 65,536 steps. Removing the multiplier revealed both primes at the fourth step. The input was built with a close match between two small multiples of its primes.

title: Combining rounded sums to recover remainders
impact: One precision schedule uses 89 sums with 53 fractional bits each. On 667, one 616-term sum sufficed to recover 23 and 29.
scope: The setup for the small example also encounters its factors. Higher precision in one sum can supply several readings.
detail: An alternative uses 89 sums rounded to 53 fractional bits each. A higher-precision sum can supply several readings. For 667 we used one sum of 616 terms to recover 23 and 29. Its setup also encounters the factors.

title: A wide-modulus sieve and its full-size cost
impact: The proposed worst-case bound excludes more guesses for similarly sized primes. The search recovered both primes of a randomly drawn 79-bit product.
scope: The full bound awaits independent review. At 2,048 bits the main sieve requires at least 2⁴⁰⁰ residue visits or table entries.
detail: For two similarly sized primes, we derive a way to rule out more guesses. The full bound awaits independent review. The search recovered both primes of a 79-bit product from random prime draws. At 2,048 bits the main sieve requires at least 2⁴⁰⁰ residue visits or table entries.

sources.label: Read the bound and its assumptions

title: Even a correct digit can leave many candidate sums
impact: At least 2⁶³⁰ sums on the fresh product and 2⁶³³ on the crossed product pass both the supplied digit and the remainder test.
scope: Two specific 2,048-bit inputs. The digit radix is at most 2¹²⁸ and the combined sieve modulus at most 2²⁵⁶. The correct digit is supplied for free.
detail: A true sum passes once in each complete repetition of its digit and sieve pattern. The proof counts distinct survivors inside the actual interval without assuming any of these other candidates have an integer-square discriminant.

title: One large-prime test leaves about half the sums
impact: Between 43.75% and 56.25% of the first 2⁵²¹ candidates in the tested progression pass.
scope: One 2,048-bit product and an independent 1,024-bit test prime. The count uses two published analytic estimates as explicit hypotheses.
detail: A surviving sum has a square discriminant modulo the chosen prime. Locating a sum with an integer-square discriminant remains a separate problem. The bound counts the survivors without scanning the window.
